questions.prompt: Why does resetting a compromised user's password NOT immediately end an attacker's active session?
options: Because the attacker's session is protected by their own MFA
Because refresh tokens are issued at sign-in time and remain valid independent of later password changes, silently renewing access tokens in the background
Because Entra ID caches passwords for 24 hours before applying changes
Because password resets only apply to new sign-ins, never to on-prem AD
questions.explanation: A refresh token was issued based on the password's validity at that moment, not the password's current value. Changing the password doesn't retroactively invalidate a token already issued — that requires explicit session revocation.

questions.prompt: What does Revoke-MgUserSignInSession actually do that the GUI password-reset flow does not?
options: It changes the user's password automatically
It forcibly invalidates the account's refresh tokens, forcing re-authentication across every mobile, desktop, and web session simultaneously
It disables the user's account entirely
It only revokes sessions on Windows devices, not mobile
questions.explanation: This is the core mechanism: refresh tokens underpin every persistent session across every app and device for that account, and this one PowerShell call invalidates all of them at once — something the GUI reset flow does not do by itself.

questions.prompt: For a hybrid (AD-synced) account, why is a single password reset not reliably sufficient?
options: Password resets are always rejected the first time for security reasons

On-premises AD is authoritative and syncs to Entra ID on a cycle — a reset made without accounting for sync timing can leave a window where the effective live password isn't what you intended, which a second, confirmed reset closes
Hybrid accounts require a manager's approval for every password change
Entra ID doesn't support password resets for synced accounts at all
questions.explanation: Because on-prem AD is the source of truth and sync isn't instantaneous, a single reset can be raced by the sync cycle. Resetting once, forcing/confirming sync, then resetting again is what actually guarantees the final live password isn't one the attacker observed.

questions.prompt: Which of these are correctly part of the full hybrid account-compromise runbook? (Select all that apply.)
options: Revoke sessions immediately, before doing anything else
Reset the password only once, to minimize user disruption
Force an Entra Connect delta sync rather than waiting for the automatic cycle
Review MFA methods registered on the account for anything the attacker may have added
questions.explanation: Immediate revocation, forcing the sync rather than waiting, and auditing MFA methods are all real steps in the runbook. Resetting only once is exactly the shortcut this lesson exists to prevent.
